item.title: How do I test an automation before I trust it?
item.dc:creator: Chinenye
item.description: Run it on five normal examples, add two messy ones, and compare each result with what you would have done by hand. Keep a human check on anything that touches money or customers. Test again after any change.
item.content:encoded:
An automation that fails loudly is easy. You see the error and you fix it.

The one that fails quietly is the problem. It runs for weeks, looks fine, and sends the wrong thing to the wrong person while you are asleep.

So you test before you trust. It takes about an hour, once.

Test with real cases, not perfect ones

Say you set up a reply that sends your price list when someone comments PRICE.

The easy test is a comment that says PRICE. It works. You feel good and switch it on.

Then a real customer comments "price pls". Another types "PRCE". Another writes "how much" and sends nothing else. If you never tried those, you find out from your customers. I wrote about exactly this in why does my Instagram DM bot break when customers make typos.

So your test list needs two kinds of cases.

  • Five normal ones. What a customer would send on a good day.
  • Two messy ones. Typos, capital letters, an empty message, a very long one, a duplicate, anything you did not plan for.

Compare it with what you would have done

For each test, write down what you expected before you run it. Then look at what happened.

Any difference is a fault until you prove otherwise. Not "close enough". If you would have sent the price list and it sent nothing, that is a fault.

Decide what a human checks

Some jobs are low risk. A weekly summary you read yourself is fine to run without much worry.

But anything that touches money, a customer's private details or a promise should be read by a person before it goes out. Start it in draft mode, where it prepares the message and you press send. Move to sending on its own later, if at all.

Know how to stop it

Before you switch anything on, write down where the off switch is.

If something goes wrong at 2 AM, you do not want to be searching through menus. One line in your notes is enough: where it lives and how to pause it.

Test again when something changes

Tools change their menus. You edit a prompt. A free limit runs out. Any of those can change what your automation does.

Keep your test list, the same seven cases, and run it again after every change. It takes ten minutes, and it is the cheapest insurance you have.

The steps

  1. Write down what the automation should do. One sentence.
  2. List five normal examples. What a customer sends on a good day.
  3. Add two messy ones. Typos, empty, long, duplicate.
  4. Write down what you expect for each.
  5. Run them and compare. Any difference is a fault. Fix it, then run the whole list again.
  6. Decide what a human reads first. Anything about money or customers.
  7. Write down the off switch. And test again after any change.

Every setup in the Starter Kit has a test checklist for exactly this, so you do not have to invent one.

Trust is not a feeling. It is a list of cases that passed.

item.title: What do I need to start using AI in my business?
item.dc:creator: Chinenye
item.description: Less than you think. One AI tool, one task you repeat every week, a few lines about your business and about 30 minutes. You do not need to code or buy anything first. Start with one job, get it working, then add the next.
item.content:encoded:
Most people think they need a plan before they start.

A tool list. A course. A free weekend. So they wait, and the waiting turns into months.

You need much less than that. Here is the whole list.

What you need

  • One AI tool. Pick one and stay with it for a few weeks. Hopping between five tools is how people end up overwhelmed.
  • One task you repeat. Something you already do every week, like writing captions, replying to the same four questions or adding up your income.
  • A few lines about your business. What you sell, who you sell to and how you talk. Three or four sentences is enough.
  • About 30 minutes. One sitting. Not a month.
  • A place to keep your prompts. Your notes app is fine. When something works, save it.

That is all.

What you do not need

You do not need to know how to code. You do not need a perfect prompt. You do not need to understand how the tool works inside.

You also do not need to move your whole business over. Nobody does that. People start with one small job and add the next one when the first is working.

And you do not need to paste anything private. An amount and a date are enough for most tasks. The rules in what should I never paste into an AI tool cover what to keep out.

Pick a boring first task

The best first task is boring and repeated.

If you do it every week and it makes you groan, it is a good one. Say you write your Instagram captions on Sunday night and you hate it. That is a better start than something clever you will use once.

Avoid anything where a mistake costs money or reaches your customers before you have read it. Start where you are the one checking the result.

The steps

  1. Write down what you do by hand every week. Five or six things is enough.
  2. Circle the one that annoys you most.
  3. Describe your business in three or four sentences. What you sell, who it is for, how you sound.
  4. Ask the AI to do a first draft of that task. Paste your description, then say what you want.
  5. Read it and fix it. Change anything that is wrong or does not sound like you.
  6. Save the prompt that worked. Next week you paste it again and skip steps 3 and 4.
  7. Repeat next week. Then pick the next task on your list.

If you want a starting point, the free AutoStack Checklist walks you through picking your first task. The Starter Kit has 36 setups once you are ready for more.

Start small. A task that saves you twenty minutes, done every week, beats a plan you never begin.

item.title: How do I chase unpaid invoices without sounding rude?
item.dc:creator: Chinenye
item.description: Write three reminders once: a friendly nudge, a clear reminder and a firm final notice. Then send the right one on the right day. The same calm words every time means you never chase money while you are annoyed. Let AI draft them in your voice, and read every message before it goes.
item.content:encoded:
Chasing money is awkward because you are afraid of sounding desperate.

So you wait. A week passes. Then two. And when you finally send the message, it comes out either far too soft or far too sharp, because by then you are already annoyed.

The problem is not your tone. The problem is that you write the message in the moment, while you are in a mood. Write it once, in a calm hour, and the mood is gone.

Why it feels rude

Asking for money you are owed is not rude. The client agreed to pay. You are reminding them of a date.

What feels rude is the guessing. Do you mention the amount? Do you say sorry? Do you hint and hope they catch it? Most people end up apologising for the invoice, which is the wrong way round.

A good reminder does four things and nothing else:

  • it names the invoice
  • it states the amount and the date it was due
  • it says how to pay
  • it asks for one thing: payment by a certain day

That is the whole message.

Write three reminders, not one

You do not need ten messages. Three is enough, and each has a different job.

  • The friendly nudge. Sent the day after the due date. It assumes they forgot, and it makes that easy to say yes to.
  • The clear reminder. Sent about a week later. Same facts, plainer tone, and a firm date.
  • The firm final notice. Sent after that. It says what happens next, such as pausing the work until the invoice is settled, but only if that is really what you would do.

Say a client owes you ₦150,000 for a design job that was due on the 1st. The nudge goes out on the 2nd. Same invoice, same amount, calm words. If nothing comes, the clear reminder goes out around the 9th. You never had to decide how you felt about it.

Let AI draft them in your voice

This is where AI helps. Give it three things: a sample of how you normally write to clients, the facts of one invoice, and the job of each reminder. Ask for the three messages.

Then read them. Change anything that does not sound like you. Do not send a message you have not read. A reminder with the wrong amount in it is worse than a late one.

Use the client's first name and the invoice number. Leave out bank details and anything private. The rules in what should I never paste into an AI tool apply here too.

Keep one simple list

The messages are the easy part. The hard part is knowing who is overdue.

Keep one list with five columns: client, invoice number, amount, due date and days late. Look at it once a week. Whoever is past due gets the next reminder in line.

The steps

  1. List every unpaid invoice. Client, amount and due date.
  2. Mark what is overdue today.
  3. Write your three reminders once. Or ask AI for a first draft in your voice.
  4. Read and edit them. Fix the amount, the date and the payment details.
  5. Send the right one on the right day. Nudge, then reminder, then final notice.
  6. Note the date you sent each one. So you never send the same message twice.
  7. Do it weekly. Pick a day and keep it.

A list of overdue invoices, with a polite reminder ready for each, is one of the setups in the Automate layer of the Starter Kit.

You are not chasing anyone. You are following a routine. That is a lot easier to do without feeling rude.

item.title: Do I need to know how to code to use AI in my business?
item.dc:creator: Chinenye
item.description: No. You can use AI in your business without writing any code. What you need is a clear task, plain words, and the patience to test. Code only comes in when you build custom automations, and even then you can start without it.
item.content:encoded:
The people who use AI well in their business are often not the ones who code. They are the ones who can say clearly what they want.

If you have been holding back because you think you need to learn to code first, you can stop. You do not. Not to start, and not to get real work done.

What you need instead

Three things, and none of them is code.

A clear task. "Help with my business" is too vague. "Write a polite reminder to a client who has not paid" is clear. The sharper the task, the better the result.

Plain words. You talk to the tool the way you would talk to a new assistant. Say what you want, who it is for, and what it should sound like.

Patience to test. The first result is a start. You read it, fix it, and try again.

That is the whole skill. Notice there is no code in it.

Where code does show up

Code comes in when you want to connect several tools so they work together on their own. For example, a message arrives in one app, gets checked, and triggers a reply in another.

Even then, many people build these with visual tools where you connect steps instead of writing code. If you are a builder who already uses a tool like n8n, that is where the Blueprint fits. If you have never used one, you do not need it to start.

A fair picture of the Starter Kit

The Starter Kit is built for people who are not technical. It has four layers: Ask, Create, Automate and Edit. Layers 1 to 3 need no code. Layer 4 has one advanced setup, and it is optional.

Each setup is written out step by step, with the prompt included and a test checklist, so you are never staring at a blank screen.

Say you have never touched any of this

Say you run a small tailoring business. You answer the same questions in your messages all day. You do not code and you do not plan to.

You can start by writing down the five questions you get most, and your answer to each. Then you ask an AI tool to turn each answer into a short, friendly reply in your voice. That is it. No code. You read the replies, fix the ones that do not sound like you, and keep them.

What about cost?

Some setups need a paid tool. That is normal. The better kits tell you what each setup needs before you start, and put the free options first where they exist. Look for that before you commit, so you are never surprised halfway through.

The steps

  1. Pick one small task. Not your whole business. One task.
  2. Write what you want in plain words. Who it is for, what it should do, how it should sound.
  3. Try it in an AI tool. Read what comes back.
  4. Fix what is wrong. Change the words you gave it, and try again.
  5. Test it with real, messy examples. Typos, half sentences, odd requests.
  6. Add the next task only when this one works.

If you want a worksheet for finding your first task, start with the free Checklist. If you want ready-made setups, look at the Starter Kit.

You do not need to learn code to begin. You need to begin.

item.title: How do I follow up with people who messaged but did not buy?
item.dc:creator: Chinenye
item.description: Keep a list of everyone who messaged and did not buy. Follow up soon, while they still remember you, with one short message and one clear question. Do not push. If they do not reply after two tries, stop.
item.content:encoded:
The people who messaged you and did not buy are the warmest list you have.

They found your page. They liked something enough to ask a question. That is more interest than a thousand silent followers. And then, most of the time, they disappear because nobody followed up.

It does not have to end there. A short, kind follow-up wins back more than people expect, and it takes very little.

Why people do not buy

Most of the time it is not a no. It is a "not right now".

They got busy. They wanted to ask someone. Their card was not with them. They meant to come back. A follow-up is not a push. It is a nudge that gives them a reason to return.

Keep a list

You cannot follow up with people you have lost track of.

Keep a simple list of everyone who messaged and did not buy. Name, what they asked about, and the date. A note or a sheet is enough. If you are saving customer details in your messages already, you have most of it.

Follow up soon

Do it while they still remember asking. A day or two later works well. Weeks later, you are a stranger again.

Say you run a small jewellery brand. Someone asked about a necklace and went quiet. Two days later you send:

Hi [name], you asked about the [item] the other day. Still thinking about it? Happy to answer anything.

That is the whole message. It is short, it is about them, and it asks one thing.

What to send

One short line. One clear question. No pressure.

A good question is easy to answer: "Do you still want it?" or "Was there something that stopped you?" The second one is useful, because the answer tells you what to fix.

Do not paste a sales pitch. Do not repeat the price three times. And do not write a paragraph.

Know when to stop

Two tries is enough. One gentle nudge, then one last friendly message if they have not replied.

After that, let it go. Chasing someone damages the goodwill you were trying to keep. You can always speak to them again when you have something new.

Check the platform's rules

Instagram has its own rules about messaging people, especially when automation is involved. Check its current messaging rules before you build a follow-up routine, so you do not put your account at risk.

What to do when they reply

Answer the question they asked, then stop.

If they say the price is a problem, say what is included, or offer the payment option you have. If they say "later", ask when would suit them. If they say no, thank them and let it go. A kind goodbye often brings people back.

The steps

  1. Keep a list. Name, what they asked about, and the date.
  2. Follow up within a day or two.
  3. Send one short line and one clear question.
  4. Make the question easy to answer.
  5. Send one last friendly message if there is no reply. Then stop.
  6. Note what people say stopped them. It will tell you what to fix.
  7. Check the platform's messaging rules.

If Black Friday is coming, this is the other half of preparing. You can read how to get your DMs ready before the sale, and then use this list after it. If you want your replies handled while you sleep, see how the DM system works.

They asked first. Make sure someone answers last.

item.title: How do I get a weekly income summary from my bank alerts?
item.dc:creator: Chinenye
item.description: Paste your week's credit alerts into an AI tool, with account numbers and names removed, and ask it to add them up and list them by day. You get one clear summary instead of adding every alert by hand. Check it against your bank or Selar, which stay the source of truth.
item.content:encoded:
Adding up your bank alerts by hand is a small job that eats a big part of your Sunday.

You scroll your messages. You find the credits. You add them on a calculator. You lose count, and start again. And at the end you are still not sure the number is right.

There is a quicker way. It does not need any special software, and it does not need you to hand over your bank details.

The idea

Your bank already tells you every time money arrives. Those alerts are text. A tool that reads text can add them up.

So you paste a week of credit alerts in, ask for the total and a list by day, and get one clear message back. Open it on your phone on Sunday night and you can see your week in one glance.

Clean the alerts first

This step matters more than the rest.

Before you paste anything, remove what you do not need. Account numbers. Full names. Anything that is not the amount, the date and a short note.

You can read more about this in the rules for what never to paste into an AI tool. The short version: an amount and a date are enough to add up a week. Nothing else needs to leave your hands.

Say you sell clothes online. Your alerts for the week might look like a dozen short messages. You tidy each one down to "Mon, ₦[amount], payment for order" and paste the lot.

What to ask for

Keep the request plain. Ask for three things:

  • the total for the week
  • the number of credits
  • a list by day

You can also ask it to flag anything that looks odd, like two identical amounts on the same day. It will not know if something is a mistake, but it can point at it so you look.

Check it, then trust it a little

The tool is adding numbers you gave it. If you pasted a wrong amount, the total will be wrong.

So treat the summary as a convenient copy. Your bank and your Selar dashboard are the source of truth for your money. Compare the total once or twice at first. When it matches a few weeks in a row, you can rely on it more.

Make it a habit

Pick one day. Sunday night works for many people. Set a reminder, paste the week's alerts, read the summary, and file it.

It takes a few minutes, and you stop carrying the number in your head.

The steps

  1. Pick a day each week. Sunday night works well.
  2. Collect the week's credit alerts.
  3. Clean them. Remove account numbers and names. Keep the amount, the date and a short note.
  4. Paste them in and ask for three things. The total, the number of credits, and a list by day.
  5. Read the summary. Look at anything it flags.
  6. Check it against your bank or Selar. Do this every time at first.
  7. Save it. One message per week, in the same place.

A weekly income check from the alerts you paste is one of the setups in the Automate layer of the Starter Kit, with the prompt and a test checklist written out for you.

You do not have to add it up by hand. You just have to check it.

item.title: Why does my Instagram DM bot break when customers make typos?
item.dc:creator: Chinenye
item.description: Most DM bots look for one exact word. If the customer writes it differently, the bot finds no match and goes silent or repeats a menu. The fix is a setup that reads the whole message, so a typo, slang or a normal sentence still gets the right answer.
item.content:encoded:
Your bot is not broken. It is doing exactly what you told it to do.

You told it to wait for one word. The customer used a different one.

That is the whole problem, and it is a very common one. Here is why it happens, and what to do instead.

What is actually happening

A keyword bot works from a list. If the message contains a word from the list, it replies. If it does not, it does nothing, or it sends the same menu again.

That works in a test. You type PRICE, it answers, and you feel good.

Then real customers arrive.

What real messages look like

People type fast, on small screens, in the middle of something else.

"How much be this one."

"Price pls."

"Is it available abeg."

"Hey saw ur ad, can i pay half now"

None of those is a clean keyword. Some have the word you wanted, spelled differently. Some have no keyword at all, just a normal sentence. A rigid bot looks at each one and finds nothing.

What the customer thinks

This is the part that costs you money.

The customer does not think, "this bot has a rule problem." They think, "nobody is replying."

So they wait a moment, then message another seller. You paid for the ad that brought them to your inbox, and they left without ever knowing a rule was the reason.

Fixes that do not work

Adding more keywords. You add PRICE, then PRICES, then PRICE PLS, then PRICE OOO. It never ends, because people can always write it a new way.

Adding a menu. "Reply 1 for price, 2 for delivery." It works until someone types a sentence, and then it fails the same way. It also asks serious buyers to do work you should be doing.

Replying yourself. It works, but only while you are awake, charged and free.

What works instead

A setup that reads the whole message and works out what the customer wants. A typo does not stop it. Slang does not stop it. A normal sentence does not stop it.

It still sends your answers, in your words. It just does not need the customer to say the magic word first. And it runs on a server, so your phone battery and your power do not matter.

Why it hurts most during a sale

On a normal week, a missed message is one lost sale. During a big sale, the same rule fails again and again, with every buyer typing the way they always do. The more traffic you send, the more of it your bot drops. That is why this is worth fixing before your next push, and not after. If a sale is coming, read how to get your DMs ready too.

The steps

  1. Open your inbox and read your last twenty messages. Read what customers really sent, not what you think they send.
  2. Mark every message your bot ignored. That list is your fix list.
  3. Replace exact-word rules with a setup that reads the whole message.
  4. Keep your own answers for the important questions. Price, delivery and payment. The system uses your words.
  5. Add a checkout link and a backup payment option. If a card fails, the buyer should see another way to pay.
  6. Test with typos on purpose. Send it ten bad messages and fix whatever it misses.
  7. Decide what happens when it does not know. An honest "I will reply in the morning" beats silence.

For the replies themselves, read what a Black Friday auto-reply should say. To see how the whole system works, look at DM automation. If you want to talk it through first, you can book a one-on-one consultation.

People type like people. Build for that.

item.title: How do I plan a month of Instagram posts in one sitting?
item.dc:creator: Chinenye
item.description: Pick four lessons you already teach, one for each week. Give each week one job: a problem, a how-to, a real story, and an offer. Turn each lesson into a few posts with a hook and a call to action, then queue the whole month in one sitting.
item.content:encoded:
You stop deciding what to post at 9 PM when the deciding is already done.

That is the whole idea behind planning a month at once. It is not about posting more. It is about not starting from zero every evening, when you are tired and nothing sounds good.

Here is a simple way to do it in one sitting.

Start with four lessons, not thirty posts

Do not try to think of thirty ideas. You will stall.

Pick four lessons you already teach. One for each week. A lesson is something you have really said to a client or a customer, not a topic.

Say you run a small catering business. Your four lessons might be: why orders get missed, how to confirm an order in one message, what to do when a client changes the date, and how to book a tasting. Four lessons. A month of material.

Give each week one job

A month feels bigger than it is. Break it into jobs.

Week one: a problem your buyer has. Name the pain. People stop when they see their own problem.

Week two: a how-to that fixes it. Show the steps. This is where you earn trust.

Week three: a real story from your own work. This one has to be yours. A client you helped, a day that went wrong, something you learned. No tool can write it for you, and it is the post people remember.

Week four: an offer with a clear next step. Say what you sell and how to get it.

Cut each lesson into a few posts

One lesson can become a caption, a short video and a longer piece. You can read how in how to turn one idea into a week of posts.

Every post needs two things. A hook, which is the first line that stops the scroll. And a call to action, which tells people what to do next: comment a word, save the post, send a message.

Queue it, then leave room

Put every post on a calendar in one sitting, with a date for each. Then leave a gap or two.

Real things happen. A customer says something funny. A sale comes up. A plan that has no room for those is a plan you will drop.

Three ways this goes wrong

You plan thirty ideas. You will stall by the tenth. Start with four lessons.

You skip your own story. A month of how-tos with no real moment from your work reads like everyone else's page.

You leave no gap. Plans with no room for real life get dropped by week two.

The steps

  1. Pick four lessons you already teach. One for each week.
  2. Give each week a job. Problem, how-to, real story, offer.
  3. Turn each lesson into a few posts. A caption, a short video, a longer piece.
  4. Write a hook and a call to action for every post.
  5. Edit it all in your own voice. Cross out anything you would not say.
  6. Add your real story to week three. From your own work.
  7. Put every post on the calendar in one sitting. Leave a gap or two.

The Create layer of the Starter Kit is built around this: four weeks of posts, each with a hook and a call to action, and your whole month queued in one sitting.

Plan once. Then spend the month doing the work, not wondering what to post.

item.title: What should I never paste into an AI tool?
item.dc:creator: Chinenye
item.description: Never paste passwords, card details, full bank account numbers, ID numbers like your BVN or NIN, API keys, or private client contracts. Paste your own lessons, public information, and examples with the names and numbers removed. When in doubt, leave it out.
item.content:encoded:
Before you ask what AI can do for you, ask what you are about to hand it.

This is the question people forget. The tool is fast and friendly, so you paste in whatever is in front of you: a customer's message, a bank alert, a contract. It feels like a private chat. It is not always as private as it feels.

You do not need to be scared of AI tools. You need a few rules.

What to never paste

Passwords and card details. There is no task where an AI tool needs these. If something asks for them, stop.

Full bank account numbers. You can paste an amount and a short note. You do not need the account number.

ID numbers. In Nigeria, that includes your BVN and your NIN. Keep them out of every chat.

API keys and login links. These are keys to your accounts. Anyone who holds one can act as you.

Private client contracts. If a client trusted you with a document, that trust does not cover pasting it into a tool you have not checked.

What is safer to paste

Your own lessons and ideas. Public information. A draft you would be happy for anyone to read. And examples where you have removed the names and numbers.

That last one is the trick. You can almost always get the help you need without the private parts.

Swap real details for labels

Say you run a small bookkeeping service and you want help writing a polite reminder to a client who has not paid. You do not need the client's name, phone number or account details.

Write: "Customer A owes me for work from last month. They have not replied to two messages. Write a polite reminder." The tool does the same job, and nothing private left your hands.

A simple test

Ask yourself: would I be happy if this appeared in a screenshot posted online?

If the answer is no, do not paste it. If you are not sure, leave it out. You can always add a label back later.

Check your tool's settings

Different tools handle your chats in different ways, and it can depend on your plan. Many have a setting that controls whether your chats can be used to improve the tool. Find it, read it, and choose on purpose. Do this before you paste anything you care about.

If you already pasted something

It happens. Do not panic, but do act.

If you pasted a password or a key, change it now. If you pasted card details, tell your bank. If it was a client's private document, be honest with the client. Then use the rules above so it does not happen again.

The steps

  1. Decide what is private. Passwords, card details, account numbers, ID numbers, keys and contracts.
  2. Remove names and numbers before you paste. Use labels like Customer A.
  3. Paste only what the task needs. An amount, not an account.
  4. Check your tool's data settings. Read them once, on purpose.
  5. Use the screenshot test when you are unsure.
  6. Test any new setup with made-up examples first. Only use real details once you trust it.

The Starter Kit puts a test checklist on every page for this reason. You can start with the free Checklist, or look at the Starter Kit.

A tool is only as safe as what you give it. Give it less.

item.title: What should my Black Friday auto-reply say?
item.dc:creator: Chinenye
item.description: A good auto-reply answers the question the buyer asked, gives them the next step, and sounds like you. Skip the 'we will get back to you' message. Write short replies for the questions you get most, with your price, your delivery details and your checkout link.
item.content:encoded:
Your auto-reply is the first thing a Black Friday buyer reads. So make it do something.

Most auto-replies say "Thanks for your message, we will get back to you shortly." That does nothing. The buyer already knows you got the message. What they want to know is simple: is it available, how much is it, and how do I pay.

What a good first reply does

Three things, and only three.

It answers the question the buyer actually asked. It gives the next step, like the checkout link. And it sounds like you.

That is the whole job. A reply that does those three things, in seconds, beats a long reply that arrives tomorrow.

Replies you can copy

Say you run a small shoe brand. These are the questions you will get most, with a reply for each. Swap the brackets for your own details.

"Is it still available?"

Yes, it is available. Which size do you need? Tell me and I will send you the checkout link.

"How much is this one?"

It is ₦[your price] for Black Friday. It comes in [sizes or colours]. Want me to send the checkout link?

"Can I pay half now?"

Yes. You can pay [half] now and the balance by [date]. Here is how it works: [one short line]. Shall I send the link?

"When will it arrive?"

We deliver to [your area]. It usually arrives in [number] days. For Black Friday, your last order date for delivery is [date].

When you do not know the answer:

Thanks for asking. I do not want to guess, so I will reply properly in the morning.

Read those again. Each one answers, then moves the buyer forward. None of them is a menu.

Put your sale details in

On Black Friday, buyers want to know when the sale ends and when they must order to get their item in time. So say it. Put your end date and your delivery cut-off in the replies where it fits, before the buyer has to ask.

What to leave out

A menu of numbers. "Reply 1 for price, 2 for delivery" breaks the moment someone types a normal sentence. Buyers type like people, with typos and slang.

A long paragraph. If it needs a scroll on a phone, shorten it.

A promise you cannot keep. If you say "we reply in minutes", make sure you do.

Test before the sale

Send your replies ten messy messages. "Price pls." "Abeg, is it available?" Half sentences. If a reply misses, fix the reply, not the buyer.

The steps

  1. List the five questions you get most. Copy them from your real messages.
  2. Write one short reply for each. Answer, then give the next step.
  3. Add your checkout link and your sale details. End date and delivery cut-off.
  4. Write the "I do not know" reply. Honest, and promising a proper answer.
  5. Set it up so the replies go out without you. A system that reads the whole message, not a menu.
  6. Test it with ten messy messages. Fix whatever it misses.

If you are still getting your inbox ready, start with how to get your DMs ready for Black Friday. If you want it built for you, see how the DM system works, or book a one-on-one consultation.

A reply that moves the buyer forward is the only kind worth sending.

item.title: How do I get my Instagram DMs ready for Black Friday?
item.dc:creator: Chinenye
item.description: Write down your offer and the questions buyers will ask, then write your answers once. Add a checkout link and a backup payment option, set up a way to send the answers without you, and test it with messy messages. Black Friday is on 27 November this year, so start now.
item.content:encoded:
Black Friday does not test your product. It tests your inbox.

Your price may be good. Your photos may be good. But when the messages start coming in, one thing decides the sale: can you answer while the buyer is still interested?

Black Friday is on 27 November this year. That sounds far away. It is not, if you want to do this properly.

What changes on Black Friday

More messages. The same questions. And buyers who want an answer now, because the next seller is one tap away.

Say you run a small shoe brand. On a normal week you get a handful of messages a day, and you answer them between other jobs. On Black Friday the same questions arrive all at once: "How much is this one?", "Is it still available?", "Does the sale cover this?", "When will it arrive?"

You know every answer. The problem is not knowledge. It is typing the same thing a hundred times while the next buyer waits.

Write your offer down first

Before you write one answer, write your offer in one place. What is on sale. What is not. When it ends. Your last day for delivery.

Do this on paper or in a note, not in your head. If it only lives in your head, you will answer the same question two different ways at 11 PM.

Then write the questions

Open your last busy week of messages and copy out every question. If you have no history, ask a friend to message you as a buyer would.

You will notice something. It is the same ten questions, in different words.

Write the answers yourself

Your answers should sound like you. Short. Clear. With the price, the delivery time and the next step.

This matters even if a system sends them for you. The system sends your words, not its own guesses.

Two ways to pay

Add your checkout link. Then add a backup, like bank transfer details, for the buyer whose card fails. Do not wait until someone is stuck at the payment step to think about it.

Test it with messy messages

Real buyers type like real people. "Price pls." "Abeg, is it available?" Half sentences. Typos.

Send your setup ten bad messages before the sale. If it breaks on one, fix the answer, not the buyer.

Decide what happens when it does not know

No setup answers everything. So decide ahead of time what happens when a buyer asks something you did not plan for.

The simplest answer is honest. Tell them you will reply properly in the morning, and save the message so you can. That is better than a wrong answer, and far better than silence.

The steps

  1. Write down your offer. What is on sale, what is not, when it ends, your delivery cut-off.
  2. List the questions buyers will ask. Copy them from your real messages.
  3. Write your answer to each one. Short, clear, in your voice.
  4. Add your checkout link and a backup payment option.
  5. Set up a way to send the answers without you. A system that reads the whole message, not a menu of buttons.
  6. Test it with ten messy messages. Fix anything that breaks.
  7. Decide what happens when it does not know.
  8. Check it once more the week before. Not the night before.

If you want to understand how this works first, you can book a one-on-one consultation. If you want it built for your business, see how the DM system works.

I would rather spend an afternoon on this now than lose sales in the middle of the sale.

item.title: How do I turn one idea into a week of posts?
item.dc:creator: Chinenye
item.description: Start with one lesson you already teach, in three to six sentences. Give it to an AI tool with your voice and a rule not to invent anything, and ask for one newsletter, three short captions and three hooks. Edit them, add one real example, and spread them across your week.
item.content:encoded:
You do not have a content problem. You have one good lesson and no time.

That is usually the whole story. You know something useful. You have said it to a client, in a voice note, in a DM. But when it is time to post, you stare at the screen and start from zero.

So here is a better way to start.

Start with a lesson, not a topic

A topic is "bookkeeping". A lesson is "keep one account for your business and nothing else".

The tool cannot make up your lesson for you. It can only reshape what you give it. Thin input gives thin posts. So the first job is yours: write or say one lesson you really teach, in three to six sentences.

Say you run a bookkeeping service for small shops. Your lesson might be: "Most owners mix business and personal spending in one account. Then at the end of the month nobody knows what the shop really earned. I tell them to open a separate account and move only what they pay themselves." That is a view, a rule and a reason. It is enough to work with.

If typing feels slow, speak it into a voice note and turn it into text. Your own rhythm is in there.

What you ask for

You are not asking for a week of posts. You are asking for a small set of things that come from one idea:

  • one newsletter draft
  • three short captions
  • three hook options for a short video

Give the tool your lesson, tell it to use your voice and plain words, and tell it not to invent stories, numbers or client results. That last rule matters more than the rest.

Where the week comes from

This is the part people miss. One lesson, cut three ways, fills a week without repeating yourself.

A caption on Monday states the rule. A short video on Wednesday opens with a hook and shows the mistake. The newsletter on Friday tells the longer story. Same idea. Different shape each time.

Edit before you post

Do not skip this.

Read each piece out loud. Cross out anything you would never say to a friend. Cross out any claim you have not really made. Then add one real example from a real client or a real day, because that is the line no tool can write for you.

Three ways this goes wrong

You paste a topic. "Bookkeeping" gives you a brochure. A lesson gives you a post.

You post it as it came. The first version is a rough cut. Treat it like one.

You let it add a story. If it did not happen, it does not go in. A made-up result costs you far more than a quiet week.

The steps

  1. Pick one lesson you already teach. Not a topic. A lesson.
  2. Write or speak it in three to six sentences.
  3. Paste it in with your voice and your rules. Plain words, and no invented stories, numbers or results.
  4. Ask for a newsletter draft, three short captions and three hook options.
  5. Edit all of it. Cross out what you would not say. Add one real example.
  6. Spread it across your week. Caption first, video in the middle, newsletter at the end.
  7. Post one edited hook and watch the response. Change one thing next time and compare.

The full setup, with the prompt and the test checklist, is in the Create layer of the Starter Kit. This post is the reason it works.

I would rather post one lesson three ways than three half-ideas once.

item.title: What happens to my Black Friday ad spend if I reply too slowly?
item.dc:creator: Chinenye
item.description: Your ads keep spending whether or not anyone answers. If a buyer messages and waits, you have paid for the click and lost the sale. Fix your reply speed first, so every message gets an answer in seconds, even when you are asleep, and only then raise your budget.
item.content:encoded:
Meta does not care that your phone battery is dead.

Your ads keep running. Your budget keeps spending. And the buyer who clicked, got curious and sent you a message is now sitting there, waiting.

That is the whole problem with Black Friday ad spend. It is not that the ads fail. It is that they work, and then nobody answers.

Where the money leaks

Picture it. You raise your budget before the sale. Messages start coming in at night. You are asleep, the power is out, or you are busy with another customer.

You paid for that click. You got the message. And you made no sale.

There are three places this usually leaks:

  • The first reply is slow. The buyer waits, gets tired, and messages someone else.
  • You type the same answers by hand. At volume, you cannot keep up, and the replies get later and shorter.
  • Payment gets in the way. The card fails, the buyer has no other option, and they leave.

None of this is about your product or your price. It is about what happens after the click.

Fix the reply first

Here is the order that makes sense. Fix the reply, then raise the budget. Not the other way round.

More budget sends you more messages. If you cannot answer the ones you already get, you will pay more for more silence.

This is also why a phone is a weak place to keep your replies. Your battery, your network and your power are all in the chain. Moving the replies to a server takes the weakest part out.

Check where you stand today

Open your last twenty messages. For each one, note how long the buyer waited for a first answer. Mark the ones that never got one.

Do not skip this. It tells you what the leak actually is, and most people are surprised by what they find.

What a good first reply does

A good first reply is not clever. It does three things.

It answers the question the buyer actually asked. It gives the next step, like the checkout link. And it sounds like you, not like a form letter.

Do those three things quickly and you keep the buyer. Miss any of them and the buyer goes back to scrolling. And on Black Friday, scrolling is the competition.

The steps

  1. Check how long a buyer waits for a first reply today. Use your last twenty messages.
  2. Mark the messages that got no reply at all. That is your leak.
  3. Write your answers to the questions that come up most. Price, delivery, availability, payment.
  4. Set up a way to send them without you. One that reads the whole message and runs on a server, not your phone.
  5. Add your checkout link and a backup payment option. If a card fails, the buyer should see another way to pay straight away.
  6. Save the buyer's contact details before you send the link. Then you can follow up.
  7. Test it with messy messages. Typos, slang, half sentences.
  8. Only then raise your budget.

If you want to understand your own leak first, you can book a one-on-one consultation. If you want the replies built for your business, see how the DM system works.

Spend on the ad after you have fixed the answer. Not before.

item.title: What should I do before Black Friday as an online seller?
item.dc:creator: Chinenye
item.description: Decide your offer and count your stock first. Then test your payment and delivery, plan your content, get your DM answers ready, and run one full test the week before. Black Friday is on 27 November this year, so start now and work in order.
item.content:encoded:
Do not start with the ads. Start with the boring list.

Most Black Friday trouble does not come from a bad offer. It comes from small things nobody checked: a checkout link that fails, a delivery date nobody confirmed, a stock count that was wrong. These are all things you can fix now, while it is quiet.

Black Friday is on 27 November this year. Work through this list in order.

Now: decide your offer and count your stock

Say you run a small bag brand. The first job is not a photo or a caption. It is a note that says what is on sale, what is not, when it ends and your last day for delivery.

  • Write down your offer in one place
  • Check your numbers, so you do not sell at a loss
  • Count your stock, item by item
  • Decide what you will do when something sells out

Everything else depends on this note. Your ads, your captions and your replies will all repeat it.

Four weeks out: test payment and delivery

This is the step people skip, and it is the one that costs the most on the day.

  • Buy something from your own checkout, start to finish
  • Add a backup way to pay, like bank transfer details, for when a card fails
  • Confirm you can see every payment as it lands
  • Ask your delivery partner what they can handle on a busy day, and set your delivery cut-off from their answer

If something breaks here, you have weeks to fix it. If it breaks on Black Friday, you have minutes.

Two weeks out: plan your content and ready your DMs

You will be busy that week. So write your posts before it starts.

  • Plan the posts for the whole week, including a few teasers before the sale
  • Write the answers to the questions buyers will ask
  • Set up a way to send those answers without you
  • Decide what happens when a buyer asks something you did not plan for

For the content, you can plan a month in one sitting, and the Create layer of the Starter Kit is built for that. For the messages, read how to get your DMs ready, then check what slow replies cost your ad spend before you raise any budget.

The week of: run a full test, then plan to rest

  • Send your setup ten messy messages: typos, slang, half sentences
  • Walk through the buyer's whole path one more time, from message to payment
  • Decide who answers what, and when you will sleep

That last one matters more than it sounds. A tired seller makes slow, short replies. Plan your rest the way you plan your stock.

After: follow up

Black Friday does not end when the sale does.

  • Thank the people who bought
  • Write to the people who messaged and did not buy
  • Write down what worked while you still remember it

The people who asked about your product are the warmest list you will have all year. Do not let them go cold.

The steps, in short

  1. Write your offer down and count your stock.
  2. Test your checkout and your backup payment.
  3. Confirm delivery and set your cut-off.
  4. Plan your content and your DM answers.
  5. Run a full test the week before.
  6. Plan your rest.
  7. Follow up after.

If you want a second pair of eyes on how your business runs before the rush, you can book a one-on-one consultation. If you want your replies handled while you sleep, see how the DM system works.

Do the boring list now. The sale takes care of itself after that.

item.title: How do I know which tasks in my business to automate first?
item.dc:creator: Chinenye
item.description: Start with the task you repeat most that needs no real thinking. Write down what you actually do for one week, then pick the one that eats the most time. Automate that one, test it, and only then pick the next.
item.content:encoded:
Do not start with the tool. Start with the task.

Most people do it the other way round. They hear about a new tool, get excited, and go looking for something to point it at. Three weeks later it is sitting there, half set up, and nothing has changed.

So here is a better order.

Picture a normal Tuesday. You answer the same three questions in your DMs. You copy a customer's details into a sheet. You type the same payment details again for someone new. By evening you have done a lot, and none of it grew the business.

And the question you would ask is: which of those do I fix first?

Look at where the hours leak

There are four places time usually leaks in a small business.

  • Lead capture and tracking. Someone shows interest and their details end up nowhere.
  • Manual work and repeated admin. The same copy, paste and retype, every day.
  • Data storage and security. Customer details sitting in places you would not want to explain.
  • Platform and audience risk. Your whole audience lives on one app you do not own.

You do not need to fix all four. You need to see which one is costing you most.

Pick the boring one

The best first task to automate is boring. You repeat it often, it needs no real thinking, and you would not miss doing it.

The worst first task is the one that needs your judgement. A difficult customer. A price you have to decide on the spot. Leave those with you.

Say you sell fabric online. Your week list might look like this: answering "is this still available?" in your DMs, sending the same delivery details to every buyer, copying each order into a sheet, posting on Instagram, choosing new stock, and calming a buyer who got the wrong colour.

Cross out choosing new stock and the wrong-colour complaint. Both need your judgement. What is left is repeat work. Of those, the DM questions and the delivery details come back every single day, so they cost you the most time.

That is your first task. Not the clever one. The one that keeps coming back.

Why one at a time

It is tempting to fix everything in one weekend. Please do not.

When you automate one task, you learn how it behaves. Where it breaks. What it does with a typo or a half-finished message. When you automate five, you learn none of that, and you will not know which one is causing the problem.

There is also trust. You will only let a system run unwatched once you have seen it get the small things right. That takes a few days of checking it yourself. Do that for one task before you add another.

The steps

  1. Write down what you actually do for one week. Not what you think you do. Keep a running list.
  2. Mark everything you repeat. If you did it more than twice, mark it.
  3. Cross out anything that needs your judgement. That stays with you.
  4. Pick the one that costs the most time. Only one.
  5. Set it up, then test it with messy input. Typos, half sentences, odd requests. If it breaks, fix the setup before you trust it.
  6. Move to the next one only when the first one holds.

It sounds slow. It is faster than setting up five things and trusting none of them.

If you want a worksheet for the first step, the free AutoStack Checklist is called Get Your Lost Hours Back. You can get it here.

Pick the boring task. It is never the exciting one that gives you your hours back.

item.title: How do I reply to Instagram DMs at night without staying awake?
item.dc:creator: Chinenye
item.description: Set up an automated DM system that reads the customer's actual message, answers it, and sends the checkout link. It runs on a server, not your phone, so a flat battery or a power cut does not stop it. You write the answers. The system delivers them.
item.content:encoded:
Most business owners answer DMs at night because they are scared of losing the sale. I get it.

But think about what that costs you.

Picture it. A customer sees your ad late at night. She asks if she can pay in two parts. Your phone is on 4%, the power is out, and you are asleep. She waits a while, then messages someone else.

That is the problem. It is not that you are lazy. A person cannot be awake all night, and your ad does not stop running when you sleep.

Why the usual fix does not work

The usual fix is a comment-to-DM button. Someone comments a word, a menu pops up, and they tap a number.

It works until a customer types a normal sentence. Or a typo. Or slang. Then the menu does not know what to do, and the customer is talking to a wall.

And the question you would ask is: so what is the better way?

What to set up instead

You want a system that reads the message the way a person would. It answers the question, then moves the customer to checkout. It has to live on a server, so it does not depend on your phone, your battery or your generator.

Say you run a fashion brand. The messages you get most are probably: "How much is this one?", "Is it available?", "Do you deliver to Abuja?", "How long will delivery take?" and "Can I pay half now?"

You already know the answers. The system's job is to send them, in your words, the moment the message lands. For "Can I pay half now?", it sends your payment plan and then the checkout link. For "Do you deliver to Abuja?", it answers and asks which item they want.

The customer gets a reply while they are still looking. You wake up to a sale, not an apology.

Decide what happens when it does not know

No system answers everything. So decide, before you switch it on, what happens when a customer asks something you did not plan for.

The simplest answer is honest. The system tells the customer you will reply in the morning, saves the message, and you pick it up when you wake. That is far better than a made-up answer, or silence.

This is also the part people skip. They test the easy questions, see it work, and go to sleep. Then the odd question comes in at 2 AM.

Why your phone should not be the system

If your customer chats live on your own phone, you depend on your battery, your network and your power. A flat phone, a light out, a generator that is not running, and your sales funnel goes quiet while your ad keeps spending.

Moving the replies to a server is not about being fancy. It is about taking the weakest part, your phone, out of the chain.

The steps

  1. Write down the ten questions customers ask most. Price, delivery, payment plans, refunds. Your own inbox already has them.
  2. Write the answer to each one yourself. The system sends your words, not its own guesses.
  3. Connect your checkout link and a backup payment option. If a card fails, the customer should see another way to pay right away.
  4. Save the customer's contact details before sending the link. Then you can follow up later.
  5. Test it with messy messages. Typos, half sentences, the way people really type. If it breaks, fix the answer, not the customer.

Do not rush step five. This is where most setups fail, and it is the cheapest place to catch it.

If you want to understand it first, you can book a one-on-one consultation. If you want it built for your business, see how the DM system works.

I would rather spend an hour setting this up once than lose a sale every night.

item.title: Why does everything I write with AI sound like AI?
item.dc:creator: Chinenye
item.description: Because AI can only reshape what you give it. Give it a thin idea and it hands back a thin, generic post. Feed it your own words, your own example and a few plain rules, then edit what comes back before you post.
item.content:encoded:
Your AI does not sound like you because you did not give it you.

That is the whole answer. The rest of this post is how to fix it.

Here is what usually happens. You open Claude or ChatGPT and type: "Write me a post about time management." The tool has nothing of yours to work with. So it reaches for the average of everything it has read. Polite. Tidy. A bit like a brochure.

You read it and think, who wrote this?

And the question you would ask is: so how do I make it sound like me?

Start with your own words, not an empty box

An AI tool can only reshape what you give it. Thin input gives thin posts.

So give it something real. One lesson you teach, in three to six sentences. If typing feels slow, speak it into a voice note and paste the transcript. Your rhythm is in there. Your odd little phrases too.

Say you coach freelancers on pricing. Here is the thin version you might type: "Write a post about pricing."

Here is the real version: "Most freelancers price by guessing what the client can afford. I price by how long the work takes and what it has to cover. If a client says it is too much, I do not drop the price. I drop the scope."

The first gives the tool nothing to hold on to. The second gives it a view, a rule and a reason. Same tool. Very different post.

Tell it your rules

Most of the "AI sound" is habits. Long sentences. Words nobody says out loud. Neat little lists of three adjectives. Cheerful endings that wrap everything up.

Write your rules once and paste them in with every request. Plain words. Short sentences. No invented stories, numbers or client results. Say the thing, then stop.

Now you want to know if the rules matter that much. They do. Without them the tool goes back to its defaults, and its defaults are what you are trying to escape.

Edit like it is your own draft

This part is not optional.

Read what comes back out loud. Anything you would never say to a friend, cross it out. Anything that sounds too sure about a result you have not had, cross it out. What is left is closer to you than anything you could get in one click.

Then add your own example from a real client or a real day. That is the line no tool can write for you, and it is the line people remember.

Four mistakes that make it worse

Asking for everything at once. One request for a newsletter, ten captions and a video script gets you one flat blob. Ask for less and you get more of you.

Pasting a topic instead of a lesson. "Productivity" is a topic. "Why I stopped checking my phone before I wrote" is a lesson. The tool needs the second one.

Taking the first draft. The first draft is a rough cut. Treat it like one.

Letting it add stories. If a story did not happen, it should not be in your post. Say so in your rules, in plain words, every time.

I know it feels slower than clicking once. But the post you edit for ten minutes is the post people reply to, and the one you click once is the one they scroll past.

The steps

  1. Write or speak one lesson you teach. Three to six sentences is enough.
  2. Paste it in with your rules. Ask for your voice, plain words, and no invented stories, numbers or results.
  3. Read the result out loud. Cross out anything you would never say.
  4. Add one real example. A real client or a real day, never a made-up one.
  5. Post one version and watch the response. Change one hook next time and compare.

The full setup for this is in the Starter Kit, in the Create layer. This post is only the reason it works.

I would rather post something plain that sounds like me than something polished that sounds like nobody.
